text: A man is dressed by other men's hands, slowly, the way people handle a thing that has to hold. He is Andrés Roca Rey, a working bullfighter, and Albert Serra gives one day of that work 126 minutes, a length no interview format would tolerate. The choice does something: the dressing and the ring get the same unhurried regard, so the day never sorts itself into ceremony and event. Nothing is explained to the camera. A viewer arrives with whatever position on the bullring they already hold, and the film makes no offer to adjust it, supplying instead proximity, held well past the point where proximity is comfortable, to a man who at every moment is still only a man in a room. It took the Gaudí for best documentary, and the Golden Shell list keeps it in view.

The rich half of the town sits up the hill, the poor half below it, and the women of the upper half bear no children. Sierra maldita, which sits on the Golden Shell list, puts that forward the way a village would, as a condition of the place rather than a problem, and then sends Juan up from the lower town after Luz, who under the terms of the local belief can give him nothing. It is a love story whose obstacle is a verdict assigned by address. Ninety-five minutes leaves room for one question, and it is not whether the curse is real; it is what the town gets from believing it, and who is quietly served by the answer. Antonio del Amo made the film in 1954, and the premise only works if the belief is taken seriously as local law. That leaves the young to test it in person.

A man goes back to the village he was born in to collect two things he believes are still there: his faith, and a woman he used to love. The errand is stated so plainly that its strangeness takes a moment to arrive, since neither item is of a kind that keeps. Otakar Vávra shot Zlatá reneta in Czechoslovakia in 1965 and gave it eighty-six minutes, short enough that the return never becomes a tour and stays what it is, a demand made on other people's memories. The film watches the gap between the village a man carries with him and the one he can actually walk into, and it stays at close range while he measures it. It carries a Golden Shell and needs no more scale than it has: one traveler, one village, and the distance between them.

A seventeen-year-old with her university applications in front of her announces that she wants to try life in a convent. Her father is moved. Her aunt Maite hears a symptom. Los domingos, a Golden Shell title, lives along the seam between those two hearings, vocation and concern, two vocabularies with no shared court of appeal. What is at stake is smaller and harder than theology: whether Ainara can be credited with knowing her own mind, and which relative gets to decide that she cannot. Alauda Ruiz de Azúa takes 112 minutes over it, long enough for a family to repeat itself in several tones of voice, which is how these conversations actually run. The exam year supplies a deadline, and the deadline is what stops the whole thing from being a discussion.

The con man's problem is not the law but the passenger in his front seat. He is working the Depression, when there is no shortage of people who cannot afford to be suspicious, and a girl who may or may not be his daughter now rides along on every job. Paper Moon won Academy Awards for its adapted screenplay and for its sound, a telling pair: the film is built out of talk, and talk like this has to be heard exactly, the beat before a price is named, the shift in a voice that decides whether a stranger buys. A third Oscar went to a supporting performance, and the title holds its place on TSPDT's 1,000 Greatest Films. Peter Bogdanovich stages the partnership as a negotiation rather than a bond, which is why the affection, when it arrives, comes in the same currency as the swindles.

Fourteen months is the number that matters, and all of it is spent underground. Leopold Soha, a burglar in Nazi-occupied Lviv, hid a dozen Jewish refugees in the sewers, and he began by doing it for his own gain. A stretch of time that long means the reason a man starts cannot go on being the reason he continues, and that arithmetic is the film's subject. Agnieszka Holland spends 145 minutes down there, which is the point of the running time: nothing is settled once, everything has to be settled again next week, in the dark, with the same people. Poland's Gdynia festival gave W ciemności its Golden Lions for best film. Holland keeps Soha's first motive in view rather than tidying it away, so the courage, when it shows, is the kind that had alternatives.

The shooting happens in a prison; the damage that lasts is done in offices. A BOPE operation inside Bangu 1, mounted to end a rebellion, produces an accusation of executed prisoners, and from there the engine of the film stops being tactical and turns bureaucratic. One officer is lifted out of the unit by the governor. Another is transferred into a military police force more crooked than anything he left. José Padilha is interested in how a scandal gets metabolized: who is moved, who is rewarded, which human rights advocate turns out to be useful to which office. Brazil placed it on Abraccine's hundred best national films and gave it the Grande Prêmio for best film. The action is loud, and most of what it carries is paperwork.

A sheet of stamps is worth precisely what a buyer can be talked into believing it is worth. That makes a counterfeit set of rare ones the ideal cargo for two con men who have just met and have no particular reason to trust each other. Fabián Bielinsky keeps the mechanics in plain sight, and most of the work turns out to be logistics rather than deceit: the right doorway, the right amount of cash on hand, knowing when to look bored. The partnership needs renegotiating every few scenes, since each man is at once the other's instrument and the other's likeliest mark. The pleasure is procedural, and the clock belongs to nobody. Argentina gave Nueve reinas the Silver Condor for best film, and it turns up in the Museo del Cine's survey of the national cinema.

Val has spent thirteen years learning every rule of a house that will never be hers. She came south to São Paulo, left her daughter Jessica in Pernambuco with relatives, and raised the son of the family she works for instead; part of the wage was that distance. Then Jessica arrives, having learned none of the rules and feeling no obligation to. Anna Muylaert's drama runs almost entirely on thresholds: which room, which chair, which tone of voice, who is offered what and by whom. Sundance gave it a special jury award, and Brazil put it on Abraccine's hundred and handed it the Grande Prêmio. It is funny in the way that only exact observation is funny, because nobody can say out loud what the guest keeps violating, and there is no villain anywhere in it, which is the difficulty.

His trade is arranging dead animals into convincing poses, which is not far from the crimes he plans and never commits. The taxidermist of El aura is epileptic, and Fabián Bielinsky builds the film around what that costs a man who prizes control: the aura arrives, then a gap, then a world that has moved on without him. Argentina gave it the Silver Condor for best film, and it appears in the Museo del Cine's survey of Argentine cinema. 134 minutes is a long stretch for a thriller, and the length goes to temperament rather than incident, because the dream of a flawless plan is really a dream of being the only person in the room who is fully awake. Then an opportunity turns up, which is the worst thing that can happen to a theorist.

Raimundo Nonato cooks, and cooking is the only leverage he has ever been able to get his hands on. Marcos Jorge follows him through social positions that would otherwise stay sealed against a man who cannot argue his way anywhere, because whoever is eating grants the cook a little standing, and standing compounds. He hones the skills and he sharpens the knives, and the film treats those as one activity. Estômago moves like a fable, which lets it state a rule plainly and then charge someone for it; the comedy is dry, the crime is matter of fact, and the question under both is who gets served first. Brazil counts it among Abraccine's hundred best national films and gave it the Grande Prêmio. Then he falls in love, which is the one appetite that does not answer to technique.

The World Cup is on, and a boy has been left among strangers in a neighborhood where he knows nobody. Both things are true of Brazil in 1970, the football and the dictatorship, and only one of them is discussed at volume. Cao Hamburger holds to what the boy is actually given: the games, the neighbors, the food, the waiting, a Jewish community he has no history with and must learn from scratch. The reason for his situation is conducted in the register adults use once they have decided that a child cannot be told. That withholding is method rather than coyness, since a national emergency reaches a boy the way it reaches any child, as adults behaving oddly. It sits on Abraccine's hundred best Brazilian films and took the Grande Prêmio for best film.

A father finds a marijuana cigarette in his son's pocket, and what he does about it is have the boy committed. Neto is a middle-class teenager; the place he is delivered to runs on corruption and cruelty, and it has no particular reason to give him back. Bicho de Sete Cabeças runs eighty-four minutes, and the compression is the argument: how few steps separate a household problem from a diagnosis, and how quickly a diagnosis becomes an address. Laís Bodanzky's subject is less madness than custody, who holds it and how cheaply it changes hands, and what a signature accomplishes that an argument cannot. Brazil placed the film on Abraccine's hundred best and gave it the Grande Prêmio. The horror is administrative, and every part of it is carried out by people with reasons.

A child has been taken, and the film keeps its eyes on the two adults who are supposed to be searching. Fernando Coimbra gives ninety-eight minutes to what panic does to a couple: questions that cannot be asked without an accusation folded inside them, small omissions that were never worth mentioning until now, the speed at which love reorganizes itself as blame. Kidnap stories usually treat the family as the base from which a search is run, and here it is the thing under examination. Each parent has an account of themselves that holds together on its own, and the accounts do not fit each other; the mismatch is where the pressure goes. It is on Abraccine's hundred best Brazilian films and took the Grande Prêmio for best film.
